newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Grain-Rain caps prices but trend seen up.
newsitem.headline: Australia Grain-Rain caps prices but trend seen up.

text.p: Good rainfall in much of Australia's eastern grainbelt toward the close of last week began to push new crop wheat prices down, while a squeeze in old crop wheat saw near-term prices spike.
Most of the trade stood back, waiting for a clearer view of domestic prospects and of the likely world wheat balance amid continued weather concerns in the U.S. and Europe.
"I call it the conundrum," analyst and consultant Brett Stevenson of Agrisk Management said on Friday.
"You're in this period where you're swapping between the worlds of production, Southern Hemisphere, Northern Hemisphere," he said.
"It's a real time of watching the weather conditions for harvest in the U.S. and Europe," he said.
But in what others hailed as a brave forecast at this time of year, futures broker Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures, presented a medium-term bullish view of world wheat prices.
Ord Minnett's view, through analyst Roger Montgomery, is based on fundamental and technical analysis and is backed by every available scrap of information on 1997 production.
From it all, Montgomery has produced lists of bullish and bearish factors.

Bullish: lower 1997 production by the main export nations, the U.S., Canada and Australia; lower U.S. production; less competition for U.S. wheat; possible frost damage to Kansas winter wheat; and delayed U.S. spring planting.

Bearish: higher global ending stocks; increased production in major importing nations, China, former Soviet Union and India; higher U.S. yields; the rise of world ending stocks to 1993/94 levels; lower U.S. domestic usage, particularly for feed; consumption seen falling more than production.
Ultimately, from this conflicting mix, Kansas damage might be the force which tips the price balance upward.
Montgomery also sees the prospect of rising prices in the charts, with a recent bullish convergence in U.S. weekly wheat prices and the mathematically-based stochastic indicator.
This suggests medium to long-term strength, Montgomery says.
Last week it rained in Australia's dry eastern states mid-way through the six-week window for wheat's winter planting.

After a long dry spell which has left Australia's eastern grainbelt on the verge of serious drought, steady rain fell in the main wheat state of New South Wales, producing falls of 10 mm to 25 mm in the state's upper west, some rainfall in the lower west, 10mm-15mm in the northwest slopes.
There was also the expectation that a large cloud mass would produce rain extending southward throughout the state and into Victoria.
Bureau of Meteorology officials told Reuters on Friday that the rain was expected to extend its range.

Longer-range private forecasters, however, said pressure-based Southern Oscillation Index and sea-surface temperature El Nino data suggested greater probability of dry weather until early 1998 than of above average rainfall.
Australian new crop cash wheat prices last week slid by A$2 to A$3 a tonne while a supply squeeze on old crop wheat pushed prices up.
The Australian Wheat Board surprised on Friday with a A$5 increase in its cash bid for Australian Standard White to A$185 delivered GrainCorp at Newcastle.
Sydney Futures Exchange wheat futures prices rose in near-term contracts over the week by A$2 to A$8 but fell in more distant new crop contracts by about A$6 a tonne.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
